lead: A random variable assigns a real number to each outcome of an experiment. Its cumulative distribution and density or mass function let you compute the probability that a measured voltage, current or bit error count lies in a range. Communication receivers work with such measurements under noise, so they need these tools to predict error rates and set thresholds. The same ideas price risk in finance and score credit in banking. This chapter reviews the rules, the common distributions and the transformation of random variables that later chapters use for noise and detection.
prereq: You need first-year probability and integration, plus Fourier transform review only for the characteristic function.

blocks.text: An experiment has a sample space S, the set of all outcomes. An event A is a subset of S. Probability P(A) follows three axioms: P(A) ≥ 0; P(S) = 1; and for disjoint events A₁, A₂, ..., P(A₁ ∪ A₂ ∪ ...) = P(A₁) + P(A₂) + ... . These axioms give the complement rule P(Aᶜ) = 1 − P(A) and the addition rule P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).

blocks.where: P(A|B) is the probability of event A given that event B occurred; P(A ∩ B) is the probability that both occur; P(B) > 0.

blocks.text: Conditonal probability updates a probability after new information. Rearranging the formula gives the multiplication rule P(A ∩ B) = P(A|B)P(B). Events A and B are independent when P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B), which makes P(A|B) = P(A).

Bayes' rule reverses a conditional: P(Aᵢ|B) = P(B|Aᵢ)P(Aᵢ) / Σⱼ P(B|Aⱼ)P(Aⱼ). The denominator is the total probability of B. In a receiver, Aᵢ may be 'bit 1 sent' or 'bit 0 sent', and B is the measured voltage. Bayes combines the prior P(Aᵢ) with the likelihood P(B|Aᵢ) to give the posterior. Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together; independent events can occur together but do not affect each other's probability.

sections.h3: Random variables, CDF, PDF and moments

blocks.text: A random variable X is a function X: S → ℝ. It maps each outcome to a real number. The cumulative distribution function (CDF) is F_X(x) = P(X ≤ x). It is nondecreasing, right-continuous, F_X(−∞) = 0 and F_X(∞) = 1. The CDF works for discrete and continuous variables.
P(a < X ≤ b) = F_X(b) − F_X(a) = ∫ₐᵇ f_X(x) dx
blocks.where: F_X is the CDF; f_X is the probability density function (PDF); a and b are real limits with a < b.

blocks.text: For a discrete variable, the probability mass function (PMF) is p_X(x) = P(X = x). For a continuous variable, the PDF f_X(x) satisfies F_X(x) = ∫_{−∞}^{x} f_X(t) dt and ∫_{−∞}^{∞} f_X(x) dx = 1. A continuous variable has P(X = x) = 0 for every x. The PDF height f_X(x) is density per unit x, not a probability. Only an area gives probability.

The mean or expected value is μ = E[X] = ∫ x f_X(x) dx for continuous X, or Σ x p_X(x) for discrete X. The variance is σ² = E[(X − μ)²] = E[X²] − μ². The standard deviation σ is in the same units as X; variance is in units squared. The n-th moment is E[Xⁿ]. For nonzero mean, E[X²] = σ² + μ², not σ² alone. For zero-mean noise, E[V²] = σ², the average power in a 1 Ω resistor.

The uniform distribution on [a, b] has f_X(x) = 1/(b − a) inside the interval and 0 outside. Its mean is (a + b)/2 and variance is (b − a)²/12. The Gaussian (normal) distribution N(μ, σ²) has f_X(x) = 1/(σ√(2π)) exp(−(x − μ)²/(2σ²)). Its mean is μ and variance is σ². The standard Gaussian has μ = 0 and σ = 1; its peak height is 1/√(2π) ≈ 0.399.

The binomial distribution counts successes in n independent trials with success probability p: P(K = k) = C(n, k) pᵏ (1 − p)^{n−k}, for k = 0, 1, ..., n. C(n, k) is the number of ways to choose k items from n. Its mean is np and variance is np(1 − p). The Poisson distribution counts rare events in a fixed interval: P(K = k) = e^{−λ} λᵏ / k!, with mean λ and variance λ. The exponential distribution models waiting times: f_X(x) = λ e^{−λx} for x ≥ 0, with mean 1/λ and variance 1/λ². Here λ is the rate, in events per unit time.
For a standard Gaussian, Φ(z) = P(Z ≤ z) and Q(z) = P(Z > z) = 1 − Φ(z). Tables give Q(2) = 0.0228. These tails set detection thresholds and error rates.

sections.h3: Joint variables, transformations and the CLT

blocks.text: Two random variables X and Y have a joint PDF f_{X,Y}(x, y). The marginal PDF is f_X(x) = ∫ f_{X,Y}(x, y) dy. The conditional PDF is f_{X|Y}(x|y) = f_{X,Y}(x, y) / f_Y(y), with f_Y(y) > 0. X and Y are independent when f_{X,Y}(x, y) = f_X(x) f_Y(y). For discrete variables, replace integrals by sums and PDFs by PMFs. Independence is stronger than zero correlation; zero correlation only removes the linear part.

A function of a random variable is Y = g(X). If g is monotonic and differentiable, f_Y(y) = f_X(x) / |g'(x)|, where x = g^{−1}(y). If g is not one-to-one, sum this expression over all roots x that give the same y. The CDF method is safer: F_Y(y) = P(g(X) ≤ y), then differentiate. Some syllabi call this 'function of random variables' or 'transformation of random variables'; it is the same idea.

The central limit theorem (CLT) says that the sum of many independent random variables, each with finite mean and variance, tends to a Gaussian. The sum's mean is the sum of the means; its variance is the sum of the variances. This is why thermal noise and many interference sources are modelled as Gaussian. The characteristic function φ_X(ω) = E[e^{jωX}] is the Fourier transform of the PDF and generates moments. See Fourier transform review for the transform pair.

figure.caption: The Gaussian curve has mean 0 and σ = 1; the uniform PDF has height 1/2 on [−1, 1]. Probability is the area under a curve, not the height at a point; the example maps 4 mV to z = 2 on this standard axis.

spec.aria: A standard Gaussian PDF and a uniform PDF on minus one to one, with area under each curve representing probability.

examples.question: A Gaussian noise voltage V has mean 0 mV and standard deviation 2 mV. Find the probability that a sample exceeds 4 mV. Use the standard normal table value Q(2) = 0.0228.
steps: Write the given values: μ = 0 mV, σ = 2 mV, threshold v = 4 mV.
Standardize: z = (v − μ)/σ = (4 − 0)/2 = 2.0. The value 2.0 is in standard deviations; it is dimensionless.
For a standard Gaussian, P(Z > z) = Q(z) = 1 − Φ(z). From the table, Q(2) = 0.0228.
Because the Gaussian is continuous, P(V > 4 mV) equals P(V ≥ 4 mV); the point 4 mV has probability 0.
examples.answer: The standardized value is z = 2.0; P(V > 4 mV) = 0.0228, about 2.3%.
examples.check:
import math

mu = 0.0
sigma = 2.0
v = 4.0
z = (v - mu) / sigma
p = 0.5 * math.erfc(z / math.sqrt(2.0))
print(z)
print(round(p, 4))
print(round(100 * p, 1))

traps: PDF height can exceed 1; only area is probability. For a continuous variable, P(X = x) = 0.
For nonzero mean, E[X²] = σ² + μ², not σ². Variance is in units squared; standard deviation is in original units.
Independent events can occur together; mutually exclusive events cannot when both have nonzero probability. Do not use P(A|B) and P(B|A) interchangeably.
In the Gaussian exponent use σ², not σ. Standardize with z = (x − μ)/σ, and do not mix Q(z) with Φ(z).
The CLT needs independent terms with finite variance. It gives an approximation for a sum, not an exact result for every sample.

quiz.q: State the three axioms of probability.
quiz.a: P(A) ≥ 0 for every event A; P(S) = 1 for the sample space S; for disjoint events A₁, A₂, ..., P(A₁ ∪ A₂ ∪ ...) = P(A₁) + P(A₂) + ... .

quiz.q: Why can a PDF have height 2 while a probability is never greater than 1?
quiz.a: A PDF is density per unit x. Probability is the area under the PDF over an interval. A narrow interval can have high density but small area, so the area stays ≤ 1.

quiz.q: V is Gaussian with mean 0 mV and standard deviation 2 mV. Find P(−2 mV < V < 2 mV).
Compare the binomial and Poisson distributions. When does Poisson approximate binomial?
quiz.a: Binomial uses fixed n trials and success probability p, with mean np and variance np(1 − p). Poisson counts rare events with rate λ, mean λ and variance λ. When n is large and p is small, binomial tends to Poisson with λ = np.

quiz.q: X is uniform on [−1, 1]. Find its PDF height, mean and variance.
How does Bayes' rule combine prior and likelihood in a bit detector?
quiz.a: P(bit = 1 | V) = f(V | 1)P(1) / [f(V | 1)P(1) + f(V | 0)P(0)]. The prior P(1) or P(0) is updated by the likelihood of the measured voltage V under each hypothesis.

quiz.q: Does zero correlation imply independence? Explain with a counterexample.
quiz.a: No, in general. Let X be uniform on [−1, 1] and Y = X². Then E[XY] = E[X³] = 0 and E[X] = 0, so covariance is 0, but Y is completely determined by X. Zero correlation only removes linear dependence; Gaussian variables are a special case where zero correlation does imply independence.

quiz.q: State the central limit theorem and give one communication use.
quiz.a: The sum of many independent random variables with finite mean and variance tends to a Gaussian with mean equal to the sum of means and variance equal to the sum of variances. It justifies modelling thermal noise as additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN).

beyond: Not for the exam. Receiver sensitivity and link budgets use the Q function to turn a noise standard deviation into a bit error rate. Software-defined radios estimate PDFs and moments from captured samples to check gain and clipping. Search 'Q function table', 'characteristic function' and 'Karhunen-Loève expansion' to go deeper into random processes. In finance, the same Gaussian tail calculation prices risk, though real returns have fatter tails.
